messages.subject: Can I get CFI indices in mirt?
messages.subject_clean: Can I get CFI indices in mirt?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all.

Can I get CFI indices in mirt?
I'm fitting my polytomous data with mirt().
But, I can get any CFI, TLI indices by default setting of mirt.

I want to get CFI indices with my polytomous data in the Full-Information Item Exploratory Factor Analysis.

How can I do that?

Here is my code.

result <- mirt(covdata, i, rotate = 'geominQ', calcNull = TRUE)
coef(result)
summary(result)
fitIndices(result, calcNull = TRUE)
residuals(result)
plot(result)

--
Blessings, Seongho.

messages.subject: Re: Comparing results of eRm and mirt
messages.subject_clean: Comparing results of eRm and mirt
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeanette,

The packages use different parameterizations for the models, so direct
comparison between them would require a little math to determine the
link for partial credit models. For instance, we can compare the Rasch
models between the packages like so:

library(eRm)
library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
res <- RM(dat)
cfs <- coef(res)
scale(cfs)

#for 'Rasch', fix the slopes = 1, estimate all the b's and latent
variance parameter
mres <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype= 'Rasch')
cfs <- coef(mres, IRTpars = TRUE)
b <- numeric(5)
for(i in 1:5) b[i] <- cfs[[i]][2L]
scale(b)

You'll notice that you have to rescale the results of the intercepts
to put them onto the same metric. They also won't be exactly the same
since eRm uses CML estimation while mirt uses MML.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: standard error in fscores(..., full.scores=TRUE)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Olivia,

I recently made the switch from reporting SE's to CI's for various
reasons. The reason primarily has to do with how the g and u SE's are
determined since they aren't symmetric about their values due to being
bounded between 0 and 1. Though I suppose it makes sense to include an
option to return the parameters with their standard errors instead.
I'll add this to the dev version the next chance I get, and it will
show up on the next major release.

In the meantime, if you are in a pinch you could find the SE's
manually through manipulating the information matrix to find the
parameter cov matrix. Use sqrt(diag(solve(model@information))) to
obtain the SE's for all estimated parameters. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I recently read "The Performance of Local Dependence Measures With Psychological Data" from Carrie R. Houts and Michael C. Edwards. http://apm.sagepub.com/content/37/7/541.short
They show that the G2 from Chen and Thissen is one of the best performing indexes.

I,m now asking me the following questions:
1) Is this Monte Carlo study really that convincing?
2) Is ist possible to conclude that their simulation for graded response models is also correct for Rasch Partial Credit Models?
3) If I calculate the model in - let´s say eRm and calculate the LD values in mirt is this correct?
4) I tried to cross check the values from an IRTPRO calculation and  mirt calculation, but they didn´t match - but I´m not sure wether I could "convince" IRTPRO to really do a Rasch PCM - maybe someone knows how to...

Hoping that this is not far beyond the scope of this group I would be very thankful for anybody "who could bring some light into my dark thoughts"...

Best

Jeanette

analysis' camp of thought, and from a model diagnostic perpective.

> 2) Is ist possible to conclude that their simulation for graded response
> models is also correct for Rasch Partial Credit Models?

Doubtful, the partial credit model is a highly constrained model
(slopes all equal to 1 and free intercepts + latent variance) compared
to the graded model (slopes and intercepts all freely estimated,
variance constrained to 1). The graded model has a much closer
relationship to the generalized partial credit model than the pcm.

> in mirt is this correct?

values as well. As far as I know I standardize the residuals in a
different way compared to IRTPRO, where it transforms the X2/G2 values
to a z-like statistic where mirt transforms to a correlation-like stat
(for further factor analysis inspecting).

Hi Phil! First, wow, mirt has come a long way from the first time you released it in cran. Congrats!
Now, the issue I am trying to address.
I have two tests with subsets of items that in theory should have the same difficulty.
The difficulty of these subsets increases.
So, for example, let's say I have a test of 25 items and if you ordered them, items 1 to 5 would demand the same ability and 6 to 10 would demand the same ability and 11 to 15 would demand the same ability.. and so on, with the ability demand of each subset of five items increasing (I am trying to explore empirically if this is the case and if it is the case by how much this increase would occur).
Ok. So now I see that ltm let me constrained parameters but I have to provide the value the parameters should be constrained to.
Mplus goes further and allows me just to declare which items would have equal parameters, but I don't need to provide the value.
And so does mirt!!!!!!
Cool. So far.
Now, one thing I observed fitting my models is that
1)I can constrain Intercept and Slope (Threshold) but not Difficulty Discrimination (even though ltm calls the intercept and slope difficulty and discrimination respectively).
2)I am able to constrain the intercept but not the difficulty. For example in mirt:

######MRE code#####
pars.1 <- mirt(data, model=1, pars=T) #to get the parameter numbers of 'd'
mod.1 <- mirt(data, model=1) #unconstrained model
#setting the constrains
const.1 <- list(pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][1:5],pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][6:10],
                  pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][11:15],pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][16:20],
                  pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][21:25],pars.1$parnum[pars.1$name == 'd'][26:30]
mod.2 <- mirt(data, model=1, constrain=const.1) #constrained model

coef(mod.2) #shows me that the 'd' parameters have been constrained as requested
coef(mod.2, IRTpars=T) #shows me that there are all different 'b' parameters within subsets, albeit different from coef(mod.1, IRTpars=T)

####/MRE code#####

I also found by accident that if I constrain 'a1' that 'a' is constrained.

I guess my question is more... what is the relationship between the intercept and the difficulty parameter (hence the subject of this post).
I have a second question about anova, but it deserves its own post.
Thanks,

Manolo

Hi Manolo,

Great to hear from you :). You were one of the first who actually got
to see the package prior to the CRAN release, so I'm glad to hear that
you are liking the new features. Indeed it has come a long way.

Just so that we are working on the same code base, I rewrote your code
to work better with the current CRAN/dev version, which supports
better syntax for constraints and also created a workable dataset.

####
library(mirt)
set.seed(12345)
d <- matrix(c(rep(-2, 5), rep(-1, 5), rep(-.5, 5), rep(.5, 5), rep(1,
5), rep(2, 5)))
a <- matrix(rlnorm(30, .2, .2))
data <- simdata(a, d, N=2000, itemtype = 'dich')
head(data)

model <- mirt.model('theta = 1-30
                     CONSTRAIN = (1-5, d), (6-10, d), (11-15, d),
(16-20, d), (21-25, d), (26-30, d)')

mod.1 <- mirt(data, model=1) #unconstrained model

mod.2 <- mirt(data, model=model) #constrained
anova(mod.1, mod.2) #ns, models are basically equivalent (give the
same likelihood, or in better terms 'are equally likely')

coef(mod.2) #shows me that the 'd' parameters have been constrained as requested
coef(mod.2, IRTpars=T) #shows me that there are all different 'b'
parameters within subsets, albeit different from coef(mod.1,
IRTpars=T)
####

The reason that constraining 'b' versus 'd' gives different results is
that when constraining the 'd' parameters (as mirt does) has no effect
on the item slope parameter a1. In the traditional IRT metric, where
logit(P) = a(θ - b) = aθ - ab = aθ + d, you can see that if you
constrain the 'd' parameter, which is just an intercept, then the a
parameter has no effect since it is an independent term.

However, if you constrain the 'b' parameter only, 'a' continues to
have an effect in the model since 'b' is also multiplied by 'a'. In a
sense, 'a' and 'b' are correlated in parameter space in the original
IRT model, but not so in the parametrization adopted by mirt (the
so-called slope intercept form). Therefore, if you are trying to model
the items to have equal difficulties in the original IRT
parametrizations you are actually simultaneously affecting the 'a'
parameters....which might not be something you want!

The only way that the two parametrization match up is when the slopes
for those respective item blocks are also constrained to be equal.
Hope that helps.

Phil

H0 is the null hypotheses that the two values are equally likely,
i.e., have the same height in the log-likelihood function given their
parameters. If the models are equally likely, but one uses more
parameters, then usually for parsimony reasons you wouldn't want to
use the more complicated model if it doesn't actually fit better given
your observed data. The X2 is actually a distance measure based on the
2*(log.likelihood_1 - log-likelihood_2), which measures how far apart
one likelihood is from another in terms of ML height, and as it turns
out is distributed as a chi-squared value in large samples.

>
> 1) Am I rejecting that the constrains are valid?

You reject saying that by including the extra parameters the data were
much more likely to be observed than when not including them. So they
contribute to how well you could theoretically reproduce the data
given only model parameter inputs.

> That is, that it is necessary to free these parameters for the model to fit
> the data better?
> My interpretation would be that mod.1 is closer to reality than mod.2, e.g.,
> it is better at explaining the data
>
> 2) Am I rejecting that the two models have indeed different fit?
> In which case it comes down to other criteria to select which model fits
> better...
> if we go by the gof statistics I would say mod.1 (although sometimes, not
> here, AIC and BIC contradict each other :-/ )
> if I think parsimony then mod.2 is a better model because it has less
> parameters to estimate.

This is a pretty debatable issue, and depends more on what the models
are being used for. You're right, AIC and BIC often differ since BIC
gives a larger penalty to smaller sample sizes than AIC. I think one
is just more conservative than the other really. Personally, if I see
the BIC lower than I'm extremely confident that the inclusion of the
extra parameters is important.

Adding parameters of course always makes the observed data easier to
reproduce, and hence decreases the log-likelihood, but you really need
to be careful since adding too many parameters actually negatively
affects the precision of all the estimated parameters.....so these
information stats try to provide a good point at which you should stop
looking for extra pars and start looking at the parameter standard
errors. Cheers.

Phil

What is happening here is that the multidimensional multiple group
model is not identified. Consider the following code from the
multipleGroup example help file:

####
library(mirt)
a <- matrix(c(abs(rnorm(5,1,.3)), rep(0,15),abs(rnorm(5,1,.3)),
rep(0,15),abs(rnorm(5,1,.3))), 15, 3)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
mu <- c(-.4, -.7, .1)
sigma <- matrix(c(1.21,.297,1.232,.297,.81,.252,1.232,.252,1.96),3,3)
itemtype <- rep('dich', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))

#group models
model <- mirt.model('
   F1 = 1-5
   F2 = 6-10
   F3 = 11-15')

#define mirt cluster to use parallel architecture
mirtCluster()

#EM approach (not as accurate with 3 factors, but generally good for
quick model comparisons)
mod_configural <- multipleGroup(dat, model, group = group) #completely
separate analyses
mod_metric <- multipleGroup(dat, model, group = group,
invariance=c('slopes')) #equal slopes
mod_fullconstrain <- multipleGroup(dat, model, group = group, #equal
means, slopes, intercepts
                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts'))
mod_notidentified <- multipleGroup(dat, model, group = group, #equal
means, slopes, intercepts
                             invariance=c('slopes', 'intercepts',
'free_means', 'free_var'))
###

The first three models appear to converge well, and when you estimate
an information matrix for them all appear to behave just fine (the
dev/next major release provides a second order tests for model
convergence now for determining if a model has converged or is even
identified). More importantly, the EM history steadily increase to a
maximum, also indicating that the model is fine. However, the last
model does not converge smoothly since in the last 10-20 iterations
you can see the log-likelihood start to increase....which
theoretically never should happen unless something is amiss. Running a
second order test with the dev version shows that the information
matrix is exactly singular, and therefore the model is not identified.

I believe for the package I was too hasty with including easy-to-use
invariance commands for multidimensional multiple group models
('free_var' and 'free_varcov' especially), so I'll have to rethink
what to do about this. In the meantime, I would recommend avoiding the
free_var like commands, and pay attention to the EM convergence
history (or update to the dev version and check the information
condition). Another trick is to use the MHRM estimation, and see what
that history looks like as well; the MHRM method tends to make
non-identified models much more obvious. Cheers.

Phil

You may want read the following reference to understand the methodology, at least for the itemtype = 'Rasch' models, since mixedmirt treats this as a special case.

De Boeck, P.; Bakker, M.; Zwitser, R.; Nivard, M.; Hofman, A.; Tuerlinckx, F. & Partchev, I. The Estimation of Item Response Models with the lmer Function from the lme4 Package in R Journal of Statistical Software, 2011, 39, 1-28

I just realized you were asking about the structure matrix. My mistake. To obtain if you just need to do a little matrix algebra.

require(mirt)
x <- mirt(Science, 2)
s <- summary(x)
str(s)

F = s$rotF #factor pattern matrix
R = s$fcor #inter-factor correlations

# we know that to make the expected correlation matrix
(Rhat <- F %*% R %*% t(F))

#so in order to get the form Rhat = F %*% t(F) decompose R into a Cholesky decomposition

Fp <- F %*% t(chol(R))
Fp %*% t(Fp) #therefore, Fp is the factor structure matrix

Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Bi-Factor Model Theory
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

This question is more theoretical in nature rather than related to R or the mirt package. Would be glad also to discuss this with the community.

Let's say that I have a sample of 500 respondents, based on balanced quota sampling, who provided their responses for a set of questionnaire items on a particular print advertisement that is shown to them. There are 5 groups of respondents and for each group, a different advertisement is shown. So, there are 5 advertisements that are used for the sample groups. The objective of the survey is to determine which advertisement has the greatest impact on influencing the buying decision (LikelyToBuy) among consumers. The survey questionnaire is consist of 22 items, each requiring the respondent to provide a rating of 1 (not agree at all) - 5 (agree totally).

Also, the 5 advertisements are from 5 different competing brands for the same product category.

The 22 items in the questionnaire can be easily grouped into concept related ideas: advertisement (e.g. attractive graphics, intereting copy, great headline, etc.), product (e.g. good quality, value for money, high performance, etc.) and brand (e.g. trustworthy, innovative, vibrant, etc.)

The approach to me seems clear - a Full-Information Item Bi-Factor Analysis and the function bfactor() in your mirt package is probably the only one in the entire realm of R that can do this for a multi-group situation (like the one stated above). I envision a General, g along side the specific factors of Advert, a, Product, p and Brand, b. Using bfactor(), convergence achieved successfully and I was able to obtain the necessary model parameters.

g - general attitude towards the brand
a - advert strength
p - product strength
b - specific attitude towards the brand

So here comes the theoretical part:

1. Is it valid, as a analysis procedure, to combine the responses from the different groups into one and perform a single MIRT to establish the latent dimensions of g, a, p and b which is then used as regression variables to predict the outcome variable of LikelyToBuy among the respondents? Ultimately, any significant differences among the respondent groups will then establish which advert is the superior one. In this approach, everyone is put on the same scale for each of the latent factor in consideration.

2. DIF - how should I consider this in the context of the above analysis? As mentioned above, the 5 respondent groups are sampled based on balance quota. Equal proportions of gender, age-group, race and location. So any possible existence of DIF would be from the different ads shown to the different groups. Does existence of DIF imply differences in the 'performance' of the ads?

The objective of the survey is to determine which advertisement has the greatest impact on influencing the buying decision (LikelyToBuy) among consumers. The survey questionnaire is consist of 22 items, each requiring the respondent to provide a rating of 1 (not agree at all) - 5 (agree totally).
>
> Also, the 5 advertisements are from 5 different competing brands for the same product category.

>
> The approach to me seems clear - a Full-Information Item Bi-Factor Analysis and the function bfactor() in your mirt package is probably the only one in the entire realm of R that can do this for a multi-group situation (like the one stated above). I envision a General, g along side the specific factors of Advert, a, Product, p and Brand, b. Using bfactor(), convergence achieved successfully and I was able to obtain the necessary model parameters.
>
> g - general attitude towards the brand
> a - advert strength
> p - product strength
> b - specific attitude towards the brand

This sounds like a good approach to the problem. The emphases and power will come from whether there is no DIF in the items so that you can save some (5-1) * (22 + 44) = 264 degrees of freedom (instead of having 2 unified slopes across groups you would have 2 unique slopes for 5 groups, and so on). The key here would be to look at the latent mean/variance differences across groups for the g factor, holding the items constant (no DIF).

>
> So here comes the theoretical part:
>
> 1. Is it valid, as a analysis procedure, to combine the responses from the different groups into one and perform a single MIRT to establish the latent dimensions of g, a, p and b which is then used as regression variables to predict the outcome variable of LikelyToBuy among the respondents? Ultimately, any significant differences among the respondent groups will then establish which advert is the superior one. In this approach, everyone is put on the same scale for each of the latent factor in consideration.

Given the outline of your study, I think this is reasonable at least at first, so long as you realize you are making a no DIF assumption. From a pragmatic point of view I think this is where you should start anyway since with N = 500 you are going to run out of df pretty quickly anyway. Again, the focus is on what happens when you free the latent means, and whether this improves the likelihood (hence indicates that latent group differences are present).

>
> 2. DIF - how should I consider this in the context of the above analysis? As mentioned above, the 5 respondent groups are sampled based on balance quota. Equal proportions of gender, age-group, race and location. So any possible existence of DIF would be from the different ads shown to the different groups. Does existence of DIF imply differences in the 'performance' of the ads?

Unfortunately unbalance quota is not what causes DIF, it's the properties within the populations themselves that cause it. For instance, in a psychopathology test for depression its well known that females have a uniform DIF effect in items that ask about 'crying'. The reason is because females, on average, simply tend to cry more, and responding highly on these items may not indicate a higher level of depression. The female participant have in factor have the same θ value as a male taking the same test, but just tend to answer in the upper extremes for these items.

Notice, however, that regardless of the proportion of males and females there is this property remains, and therefore as little to do with the sampling method chosen. If you were trying to obtain test properties for the entire mixed population, ignoring specific person level attributes such as gender and race, then it would make more sense to randomly sample from this population directly rather than focus on a balanced quota design. This would allow you to make a more unbiased construction of a test, conditional on the entire population (and therefore, in general, applicable to all, but certainly not optimal for some specific subgroups; it may in fact be very wrong if the groups marginalized over are highly discrepant, but using this approach you should be able to find DIF for those groups fairly easily).

Just a technical reminder as well: while bfactor() supports MG analysis, you should be careful in how it is set up since the specific factor latent means/variance cannot be freed. This is due to the method of integration which the function capitalizes on, a cost of which is a less flexible model. Not that this matters in this case really, and it's probably better that way anyway given the identification problems with freeing multiple latent parameters in multidimensional models. Cheers.

Phil

Hi Olivia,

The issue is that the information matrix estimated from the S-EM algorithm is not positive definite. Therefore when it is inverted to find the large sample parameter covariance matrix some of the diagonal terms become negative (negative variance of course make no sense). Unfortunately this has little to do with the model itself, and has more to do with the imprecision in the S-EM algorithm for building the observed information matrix (inspect x2r@information to see what I mean, at the very least you'll notice the matrix isn't symmetric, which in itself is an issue). NaN is a place-holder indication the parameter variance was less than 0, and therefore not defined.

Currently there are only 3 SE.types that behave well under regular conditions, 'BL', 'Fisher', and 'crossprod'. I don't find it necessarily troubling though, since you could always bootstrap your model with boot.mirt() to obtain SE's that way, or estimate only the NaN parameters using a profile-likelihood approach via PCLI.mirt(). It's more just annoying, and has given me questions on whether I should provide an option to smooth this matrix before computing the standard errors.

When the S-EM algorithm works it works well, otherwise you have to resort to other methods to patch it up. Hope that helps.

Phil

Hi Edy,

I see what you mean now, thank you for clarifying. This problem exists in standard factor analysis as well, and has to do with the rotational/estimation indeterminacy problem. Basically the idea is this, if you estimated your unidimensional model with all negative starting value slopes, the solution would converge to the same values. However, the slopes would have their signs completely flipped because.

So if you had the slopes a1 = (1.5, 0.5, 0.6, 1.2, ....) this would fit exactly as well as a1 = (-1.5, -0.5, -0.6, -1.2, ....). What you've noticed is that after rotation the signs of one of the factor will mainly be negatives, giving the opposite pattern of factor scores you wanted. It's not an issue, since you always can switch the signs manually if you see that in summary(mod) there are too many negatives in the loadings for your liking.

That being said, I must have changed something on the dev version since the first factor seems to be mostly positive for these data, so the issue doesn't seem to arise. Nevertheless, it's always possible to have this happen during estimation and rotation, so it's good to know about. Here's what I get on the latest dev version, and you'll probably notice the signs are different in your summary() statement.

Phil

Hi Alexander,

Great to hear from you again. Yes this is possible by editing the initial data.frame of parameter values. You can obtain this by passing the argument pars = 'values', edit this data.frame, and input it back into the function.

###
sv <- mirt(data, model, pars = 'values')
sv$est[fixedindex] <- FALSE
sv$value[valueindex] <- 1
mod <- mirt(data, model, pars = sv)
###

It's also possible to free the latent parameter this way as well. If you have a particular format that you are looking for, using sv <- edit(sv) is probably easiest way to edit the data.frame manually through the R GUI editor. Hope that helps.

Phil

Hi Edy,

Part of the reason is some of the package internals in the M-step have changed to help in approximating the S-EM based information matrix. To get more consistent estimates, pass a smaller tolerance criteria such as TOL = 1e-5. The important thing to look for is that the log-likelihood doesn't change any more regardless of how small the TOL value is, and this location should be consistent across versions. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chun-Hsein,

When you consider the number of items, this makes perfect sense. You
have only 11 items to identify 3 cross-loaded factors, which means
that the amount of information any one item tells you about a factor
is even less than the unidimensional case. The RMSD makes sense here
as well, where the lowest difference occurs for the factor with the
largest number of loadings.

> sqrt(apply((fullscores - Theta)^2, 2, mean))
       F1        F2        F3
0.6842767 1.0985522 0.9480303

And when you consider the marginal reliability estimates by calling
just fscores() by itself:

> x = fscores(simmod)

Method:  EAP

Empirical Reliability:
    F1     F2     F3
0.6154 0.1859 0.2402

It's easy to see that the factors are pretty unreliable, and therefore
the factor scores (i.e., true-scores) are going to be measured with a
large amount of imprecision. The more items you have in a test the
more accurate you can measure factors, and factors with a smaller
number of loadings will naturally have less precision as well.

Phil
